sections.h2: Where are Osceola County property records kept?
sections.html:
Deeds and mortgages for Osceola County end up at one counter: the clerk who also serves as county comptroller and recorder. The county government site describes the clerk's duties as split between clerk of the circuit and county courts and county recorder, and it points residents to osceolaclerk.com for recording forms, eRecording, tax deeds and property fraud alerting.

The clerk's FAQ explains that everything recordable goes into a single running series labeled the Official Records. The series is permanent and a record leaves it only by court order. A separate office, the Property Appraiser, sits at 2505 E. Irlo Bronson Memorial Highway in Kissimmee, and it handles parcel values and exemptions.

sections.h2: What documents does the Osceola clerk record?
sections.html:
The clerk records deeds, leases, mortgages, liens, judgments and many other instruments that touch real or personal property. The clerk's FAQ lists several kinds, drawn from state law.

  • Deeds, mortgages, notices or claims of lien, and their releases and satisfactions
  • Notices of lis pendens, which warn that a lawsuit affects a property
  • Judgments and their assignments, releases and satisfactions
  • Federal tax liens and certificates that release them
  • Certified death certificates and military discharge records

For a seller, the lis pendens and the judgment entries deserve a look. A pending foreclosure case will show up as a lis pendens against the parcel, and a recorded judgment can attach to land you own.

sections.h2: What are the Osceola County recording requirements for a deed?
sections.html:
A deed must meet the clerk's formal checklist or it can be rejected until corrected. The clerk's page cites Florida Statute 695.26 and lists what the face of the document needs.

  • The grantor's signature notarized, with name and address printed below it
  • Two witnesses, with printed names; for documents on or after January 1, 2024, witness post office addresses too
  • A complete legal description of the property
  • The grantee's mailing address and the preparer's name and address, using a person's first and last name and not just a business name
  • A 3 by 3 inch blank space at the top right corner for the clerk's use
  • Original ink signatures, since photocopies are refused

Title searches are not a clerk service; the office refers people to title agencies and attorneys.

sections.h2: What fees does the Osceola clerk charge for a filing?
sections.html:
The clerk's schedule opens with $10.00 for page one and $8.50 for every page after it, with deed stamps on top at $0.70 per $100.

Osceola County Clerk recording and copy fees as listed in the clerk's recording FAQ
ItemFee
Recording, first page$10.00
Recording, each added page$8.50
Indexing after four names$1.00 per name
Deed documentary stamps$0.70 per $100 or fraction
Mortgage documentary stamps$0.35 per $100 or fraction
Intangible tax$0.20 per $100 on the entire amount
Copies$1.00 per page
Certification$2.00 per document

Even a deed that shows token consideration owes the minimum stamp of $0.70.

sections.h2: How do I pay and when is the office open?
sections.html:
The Recording Department accepts business checks, cashier's checks, money orders or cash, and it does not accept personal checks. Plastic is taken only at the counter, with a 3.5 percent surcharge.

Find the counter upstairs in the Judge Jon B. Morgan Courthouse, 2 Courthouse Square, Kissimmee, FL 34741. Doors are open on weekdays through the afternoon, yet the recording window closes at 4:30 p.m., and anything that arrives later is recorded the next business day. The recording phone line is (407) 742-3517. Mail a deed with a self-addressed, postage-paid return envelope.

The clerk also takes e-recordings, and the main line is 407-742-3500.

sections.h2: How do I search Osceola County Official Records and order copies?
sections.html:
The clerk runs an online Official Records search, and it is open around the clock. Copies can be bought in person, electronically, or through PERCH Search or MyFloridaCounty, at $1.00 per page, with $2.00 more to certify each instrument. Plat copies are $5.00 per page.

One safeguard costs nothing: the clerk's Property Fraud Alert. Because the office cannot check who actually signs a paper it is handed, and only a judge can order a bad filing struck, an alert that pings you on new filings under your name is cheap protection while you prepare to sell.

sections.h2: What should I do if a bad document shows up on my Osceola property?
sections.html:
Report it, because the clerk cannot pull a filing without a court order. The clerk's FAQ suggests contacting the Kissimmee Police Department, the St. Cloud Police Department or the Osceola County Sheriff's Office, depending on where the home sits, and it notes that documents spanning several Florida locations may go to the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

The same page says that section 817.535 of the Florida Statutes makes recording a fraudulent instrument against property a third degree felony, and that a court may order a fraudulent document voided and removed. A seller who finds a surprise entry should tell the title agent right away, since a buyer's lender will not close over an unexplained lien or deed.

sections.h2: What do Osceola tax records and tax deeds mean for a sale?
sections.html:
Unpaid real estate tax in Osceola becomes delinquent at the start of April and picks up a 3 percent addition. Certificates for those parcels are auctioned online by June 1, and bids begin at 18 percent and fall.

The clerk holds tax deed sales online. A certificate left alone can support a tax deed application from April 1 of the second year after purchase. On the clerk's page, the winner forfeits a deposit if they walk away, set at the greater of 5 percent of the bid or $200, and has a day to deliver the balance. Tax deed land is sold as is, and the clerk warns that it carries no promise of clear title.

Overbid money after a sale can be claimed with an affidavit sent to the clerk's Tax Deed Department.

sections.h2: What dates matter on an Osceola County tax bill?
sections.html:
The Osceola County Tax Collector's calendar runs on a few fixed dates. Payments open in November at a 4 percent discount, stepping to 3, 2 and 1 percent through February, with the gross amount owed in March.

New requests to join the quarterly installment plan must be in by April 30. Installments then fall on June 30, September 30 and December 31. An installment that misses July 31 loses its discount, adds a 5 percent penalty and ends the plan.

  • April 1: delinquent, with 3 percent added to the gross amount
  • Three weeks of newspaper advertising before the certificate sale
  • On or before June 1: online tax certificate sale
  • Redemption on or after June 1 adds a $6.25 fee

Interest on a sold certificate follows the rate at which it sold, so get the payoff in writing for your own closing day.

faqs.q: Which office records deeds in Osceola County?
faqs.a: The Osceola County Clerk of the Circuit Court and County Comptroller, acting as county recorder. The office is at 2 Courthouse Square in Kissimmee and records deeds, mortgages, liens and judgments.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a one-page deed in Osceola County?
faqs.a: The clerk lists $10.00 for the first page, plus documentary stamp tax of $0.70 per $100 of consideration. Each added page costs $8.50, and names beyond four cost $1.00 each for indexing.

faqs.q: Can I pay with a personal check at the Osceola recording counter?
faqs.a: No. The clerk takes business checks, cashier's checks, money orders and cash, and credit cards in person with a 3.5 percent fee. Personal checks are not accepted.

faqs.q: What time must I submit a deed in Osceola County?
faqs.a: Before 4:30 p.m. on a business day. The office stays open until 5:00 p.m., but recording stops at 4:30, and later documents are recorded the next business day.

faqs.q: Can the clerk remove a fraudulent deed from the records?
faqs.a: Not on its own. The clerk says it can remove a recorded item only under a court order. Report suspected fraud to law enforcement, and consider the clerk's free Property Fraud Alert, which tells you when a document is recorded against your name.
